summary: Declining a customer's request so they stay a customer: the no in one clear line, the real reason, what you can do instead, and how to grant an exception without making it the new rule.
body:
# Saying no to a customer request without losing the customer

## Goal
The customer gets a clear answer, understands it is not personal, and leaves with something: an alternative, a timeline, or a genuine explanation. A clean no keeps more customers than a vague maybe.

## Structure
1. **Thank them for the specific ask.** One line, no gush. "Thanks for suggesting this" or "Good question".
2. **The no, plainly, in the first two sentences.** "We can't do a custom size on this one."
3. **The real reason in one line.** Cost, quality, capacity, fairness to other customers. Not "policy".
4. **What you can do.** An alternative, a partial, a future date, or a referral to someone who does it.
5. **Leave the door open** without promising: "If that changes, I'll tell you."

## Principles
- Say "can't" or "don't", not "unable to at this time". Vague nos invite a second ask.
- "Policy" is not a reason. Say what the policy protects: "we close returns at 30 days because after that we can't resell the item".
- Offer what you can before they ask for it. Reactive concessions feel extracted; proactive ones feel generous.
- If you are going to bend the rule, decide fast and say it is an exception, so it does not become the new baseline. "I'll do it this once because you've been with us since 2021. Going forward, the window is 30 days."
- Bend for good reasons: long-standing customer, your own mistake, a genuinely edge case. Do not bend for volume of complaint. If you reward pressure you will get more pressure.
- Support tickets can run five sentences. DMs run two or three. Match the channel.
- Never say a feature is "on the roadmap" unless it is.

## Examples

**Feature request, support ticket:**
> Hi Lena, thanks for the detailed suggestion about bulk export to CSV. We're not building it this year; the team is focused on the mobile app and I'd rather tell you that than leave you waiting. What works today: the API can pull the same data (docs here [link]), and I'm happy to send a short script that does the export if that helps. I've logged your request against the feature so you'll get an email if it ships.
> Omar

**Custom order, DM:**
> Thanks for asking! I don't do custom sizes on the ceramic planters, the kiln setup makes one-offs cost more than anyone would pay for them. The closest I have is the 22cm, which fits most windowsills. If you want, send me a photo of the spot and I'll tell you honestly whether it'll work.

**Rush job, email:**
> Hi Dan, I can't turn this around by Friday. To do it properly takes six working days and I have two projects ahead of you. What I can do: deliver on Wednesday the 18th, or, if Friday is fixed, do the first section only by Friday and the rest the following week. Which is more useful?
> Ruth

**Expired discount code, support reply:**
> Hi Sam, that code ended on 30 June, so it won't apply to this order. What I can do: the SUMMER10 code is live until the 15th and takes 10% off, which is close to the same. Here's the link with it applied [link]. If you already paid full price, reply with the order number and I'll refund the difference.

**Return outside the window, ticket:**
> Hi Jess, the return window on this is 30 days and the order was delivered 47 days ago, so I can't take it back for a refund. I can offer store credit for the full amount, valid for a year, or a 30% discount on a replacement if the fit was the problem. Which would you prefer?

**Return outside the window, exception granted:**
> Hi Jess, the return window is 30 days and this is at 47, so normally this would be a no. Since you've ordered from us six times and never returned anything, I'll make an exception this once and refund it in full. Label attached. Going forward the 30 days is firm, just so there's no surprise next time.

**Request that violates policy (reselling, sharing an account, a discount on behalf of someone else):**
> Thanks for asking rather than just doing it. I can't add a second login to your personal plan; the personal plan is one seat and the team plan exists exactly for this. The team plan for two people is $18 a month, $6 more than you pay now, and I can apply the upgrade with the rest of this month free. Want me to do that?

**Request you simply do not do, DM:**
> I don't do wholesale, sorry, it's just me and a small kiln! If you're after larger quantities, [maker] does similar work at volume and I'd happily introduce you.

## Avoid
- "Unfortunately" and "I'm afraid" as openers.
- "Our policy states."
- A soft maybe that leaves them waiting for a yes.
- Explaining internal constraints in detail.
- Apologising more than once.
- Blaming the customer for asking.
- Granting an exception without saying it is one.
- "On the roadmap" when it is not.

## If they push back
Restate the no in one line, repeat the alternative, and do not add new reasons. "I understand, and the answer's still that I can't refund it. The store credit is yours whenever you want it." If they escalate to "I'll leave a bad review", do not change the answer because of the threat: "That's your call. I'd still like to sort this with the store credit or the exchange, and either is ready when you are." If they bring a genuinely new fact (the item was faulty, your site gave wrong information), reconsider on that fact and say that is why: "That changes it. If the size guide said 42, I'll take it back."
